chapter-map: Concept map of the book's main ideas, drawn as rounded green boxes joined by labeled arrows, with two yellow boxes, "Unit tests" and "Integration tests", near the center. Each green box names a concept and the chapter that covers it. From "Unit tests", arrows labeled "Maximize" point left to "Fast feedback (ch. 4)" and "Maintainability (ch. 4)", and an arrow labeled "Cover" points right to "Domain model and algorithms (ch. 7)", which has an arrow labeled "Have high" pointing up to "Complexity (ch. 7)". From "Integration tests", arrows labeled "Maximize" point left to "Protection against regressions (ch. 4)" and "Resistance to refactoring (ch. 4)", and an arrow labeled "Cover" points down to "Controllers (ch. 7)", which has an arrow labeled "Have large number of" pointing down to "Collaborators (ch. 2)". On the left, "Test accuracy (ch. 4)" has two arrows labeled "Defined by", one to "False negatives (ch. 4)" and one to "False positives (ch. 4)"; "False negatives" has an arrow labeled "Tackled by" to "Protection against regressions", and "False positives" an arrow labeled "Tackled by" to "Resistance to refactoring". In the lower left, "Mocks (ch. 5)" has an arrow labeled "Damage if used incorrectly" up to "Resistance to refactoring", a long arrow labeled "Used in" up to "Integration tests", an arrow labeled "Should not be used for" to "Managed dependencies (ch. 8)", and an arrow labeled "Should be used for" to "Unmanaged dependencies (ch. 8)". "Managed dependencies" and "Unmanaged dependencies" each have an arrow labeled "Are" to "Out-of-process dependencies (ch. 2)", which has an arrow labeled "Are" up to "Collaborators". "In-process dependencies (ch. 2)" also has an arrow labeled "Are" pointing to "Collaborators".
figure-1.1: Line chart. The vertical axis is labeled "Work hours spent" and the horizontal axis "Progress". A solid curve labeled "Without tests" starts near the bottom, stays low at first, then rises steeply and ends near the top of the chart. A dashed straight line labeled "With tests" starts higher than the solid curve and rises gently. The two lines cross part way along the progress axis; after the crossing, the "Without tests" curve needs far more work hours for the same progress.
figure-1.2: Line chart, an extension of figure 1.1. The vertical axis is labeled "Work hours spent" and the horizontal axis "Progress". Three lines: a solid black curve "Without tests" that starts lowest and then rises most steeply; a solid gray curve "With bad tests" that starts a little higher, rises more slowly at first, but also bends sharply upward later; and a dashed straight line "With good tests" that starts highest and rises gently. All three meet at about the same point, after which "Without tests" and "With bad tests" both climb far above "With good tests".
figure-1.3: A formula: "Code coverage (test coverage) =" a fraction with "Lines of code executed" above the line and "Total number of lines" below it.
figure-1.4: A formula: "Branch coverage =" a fraction with "Branches traversed" above the line and "Total number of branches" below it.
figure-1.5: Flowchart with four rounded boxes. "Start" at the top has two arrows leading out of it: the left one goes down to "Length > 5", the right one to "Length <= 5". Both of those boxes have arrows leading to "End" at the bottom. The two paths through the method form a diamond shape.
figure-1.6: Flowchart. "Start" leads down to "int.Parse". From "int.Parse" four arrows branch out to four lighter gray boxes in a row: "null", "“ ”" (an empty string), "“5”", and "“not an int”". Each of the four boxes has an arrow leading to "End" at the bottom. A curly brace to the right of the row of four boxes is labeled "Hidden part", marking these branches inside int.Parse as invisible to coverage metrics.
figure-2.1: Diagram in two parts, separated by a wide horizontal brace and a thick gray arrow pointing down. In the top part, a dark rounded square labeled "System under test" has two arrows pointing right to two dark filled circles labeled "Dependency 1" and "Dependency 2". In the bottom part, the same dark square, again labeled "System under test", has two arrows pointing to two white, unfilled circles labeled "Test double 1" and "Test double 2", which take the places of the two dependencies.
figure-2.2: Diagram with two dashed rounded rectangles side by side. The left one, labeled "Unit tests" underneath, contains three gray diamonds labeled "Class 1 Tests", "Class 2 Tests" and "Class 3 Tests". The right one, labeled "Production code", contains three dark rounded squares labeled "Class 1", "Class 2" and "Class 3". A thin gray arrow leads from each diamond to its matching class: "Class 1 Tests" to "Class 1", "Class 2 Tests" to "Class 2", and "Class 3 Tests" to "Class 3".
figure-2.3: Diagram centered on a dark rounded square labeled "System under test". A white rounded box labeled "Test" below it has an arrow pointing up to the system under test. From the system under test, three arrows lead out: up to a dark circle labeled "Another class", left to a faded gray database icon labeled "Database", and right to a faded gray floppy-disk icon labeled "File system". Bold annotations attached by dashed lines to the arrows mark the arrow to "Another class" as "Private dependency; keep", and the arrow to "Database" and the arrow to "File system" each as "Shared dependency; replace".
figure-2.4: Tree diagram of circles. At the top, a dark circle labeled "Dependency" has arrows down to two dark circles: one on the left marked "Shared" and one on the right labeled "Private". "Private" in turn has arrows down to two light gray circles, "Mutable" on the left and "Value object" on the right. A solid outline encloses the "Shared" circle and its label; a bold annotation on a solid line marks this outline as "Replaced in the classic school". A larger dashed outline encloses both the "Shared" circle and the "Mutable" circle; a bold annotation on a dotted line marks it as "Collaborator, replaced in the London school". "Private" and "Value object" lie outside both outlines.
figure-2.5: Venn diagram of two overlapping circles. The left, darker gray circle is labeled "Shared dependencies"; the right, lighter gray circle is labeled "Out-of-process dependencies". Three bold labels point into the regions: "Singleton" into the part of the left circle outside the overlap, "Database" into the overlap, and "Read-only API service" into the part of the right circle outside the overlap.
figure-2.6: Diagram showing the scope of three kinds of tests. In the center, a dark rounded square labeled "System under test" has an arrow up to a dark circle labeled "Another class", an arrow left to a faded gray database icon labeled "Database", and an arrow right to a faded gray cloud icon labeled "Payment gateway". A solid outline encloses only the system under test and the other class; a bold annotation labels it "Unit test". A larger dashed outline encloses those two plus the database; a bold annotation on a dotted line labels it "Integration test". A curly brace under all three bottom labels, spanning the database, the system under test and the payment gateway, is labeled "End-to-end test".
figure-3.1: Flowchart of five rounded boxes arranged as a staircase descending from top left to bottom right, each joined to the next by an elbow arrow pointing down into it: "Arrange the test", then "Act", then "Assert", then "Act some more", then "Assert again".
figure-3.2: Tree diagram of squares in three levels. At the top, a dark square labeled "Application" has arrows down to three dark gray squares, "Behavior 1", "Behavior 2" and "Behavior N", with "…" between "Behavior 2" and "Behavior N" standing for further behaviors. The bottom level holds lighter gray squares for facts. "Behavior 2" has three arrows down, to "Fact 1", "Fact 2" and "Fact N", with "…" between "Fact 2" and "Fact N". "Behavior 1" has an arrow leading down and left to a "…" at the far left of the bottom row, and "Behavior N" an arrow leading down and right to a "…" at the far right. A curly brace beneath "Fact 1" and "Fact 2" is labeled "Can be grouped".
figure-4.1: Diagram. On the left is a dark rounded square labeled "Client". In the middle, an irregular rounded outline labeled "System under test" contains three circles, "Step 1", "Step 2" and "Step 3". An arrow goes from "Client" to "Step 1", arrows go from "Step 1" to "Step 2" and from "Step 2" to "Step 3", and an arrow goes from "Step 3" back to "Client". On the right, a white rounded box reads "Test: “Are these steps correct?”"; three dashed lines run from it to each of the three step circles.
figure-4.2: Two diagrams side by side, separated by a vertical line, each with the same setup: a dark rounded square labeled "Client" and an irregular outline labeled "System under test" containing circles "Step 1", "Step 2" and "Step 3", with arrows from "Client" to "Step 1", from "Step 1" to "Step 2", from "Step 2" to "Step 3", and from "Step 3" back to "Client". In the left diagram, a white box reading "Good test: “Is the end result correct?”", with the word "Good" underlined, is joined by a single dashed line to the arrow returning from "Step 3" to "Client". In the right diagram, a white box reading "Bad test: “Are these steps correct?”", with the word "Bad" underlined, is joined by three dashed lines to the three step circles.
figure-4.3: Table with gray-shaded cells. The top-left cell reads "Table of error types". The column header "Functionality is" spans two columns, "Correct" and "Broken". The row header "Test result" spans two rows, "Test passes" and "Test fails". The four result cells are: for "Test passes" and "Correct", "Correct inference (true negatives)" in medium gray; for "Test passes" and "Broken", "Type II error (false negative)" in dark gray; for "Test fails" and "Correct", "Type I error (false positive)" in dark gray; for "Test fails" and "Broken", "Correct inference (true positives)" in medium gray. A bold annotation to the right, attached by a line to the "Type II error" cell, reads "Protection against regressions"; a bold annotation below, attached by a line to the "Type I error" cell, reads "Resistance to refactoring".
figure-4.4: A formula: "Test accuracy =" a fraction with "Signal (number of bugs found)" above the line and "Noise (number of false alarms raised)" below it.
figure-4.5: Line chart with thick arrow-shaped axes. The vertical axis is labeled "Effect on the test suite" and the horizontal axis "Project duration". Both curves start at the origin. A solid curve labeled "False negatives" rises steeply right away and then levels off near the top. A dashed curve labeled "False positives" stays near the bottom at first, then rises in an S shape and levels off just below the solid curve at the right end.
figure-4.6: Venn diagram of three overlapping gray circles: "Resistance to refactoring" at the top, "Protection against regressions" at the lower left, and "Fast feedback" at the lower right. A bold label "End-to-end tests" points to the region where "Resistance to refactoring" and "Protection against regressions" overlap, outside "Fast feedback".
figure-4.7: Venn diagram of three overlapping gray circles: "Resistance to refactoring" at the top, "Protection against regressions" at the lower left, and "Fast feedback" at the lower right. Two bold labels point into the pairwise overlaps: "End-to-end tests" to the region where "Resistance to refactoring" and "Protection against regressions" overlap, outside "Fast feedback", and "Trivial tests" to the region where "Resistance to refactoring" and "Fast feedback" overlap, outside "Protection against regressions".
figure-4.8: Venn diagram of three overlapping gray circles: "Resistance to refactoring" at the top, "Protection against regressions" at the lower left, and "Fast feedback" at the lower right. Three bold labels point into the pairwise overlaps: "End-to-end tests" to the overlap of "Resistance to refactoring" and "Protection against regressions", "Trivial tests" to the overlap of "Resistance to refactoring" and "Fast feedback", and "Brittle tests", below the diagram, to the overlap of "Protection against regressions" and "Fast feedback". Each region lies outside the third circle.
figure-4.9: Venn diagram of three overlapping gray circles: "Resistance to refactoring" at the top, "Protection against regressions" at the lower left, and "Fast feedback" at the lower right. A bold label "Unreachable ideal" points into the small central region where all three circles overlap.
figure-4.10: Diagram of a triangle with a gray circle at each corner. The top circle, labeled "Resistance to refactoring", contains the text "Max out". The bottom-left circle is labeled "Protection against regressions" and the bottom-right circle "Fast feedback"; both are empty. Off to the upper right, apart from the triangle, a fourth gray circle labeled "Maintainability" also contains "Max out". Below the triangle's base, a white double-headed arrow spans from the "Protection against regressions" side to the "Fast feedback" side and is labeled "Choose between the two".
figure-4.11: Pyramid divided into three horizontal bands: the narrow top band labeled "End-to-end", the middle, darkest band labeled "Integration tests", and the widest bottom band labeled "Unit tests". A curly brace under the pyramid's base is labeled "Test count". To the right, a vertical arrow pointing upward along the height of the pyramid is labeled "Emulating user".
figure-4.12: Diagram of a triangle with a gray circle at each corner: the top circle, labeled "Resistance to refactoring", contains the text "Max out"; the bottom-left circle is labeled "Protection against regressions" and the bottom-right circle "Fast feedback", both empty. Below the triangle's base, a white double-headed arrow pointing left and right carries three small gray sliders, which dashed lines label, from left to right, "End-to-end", "Integration" and "Unit tests"; "End-to-end" sits nearest the "Protection against regressions" end and "Unit tests" nearest the "Fast feedback" end.
figure-5.1: Hierarchy diagram. A dark rounded box at the top is labeled "Test double". Below it sit two rounded boxes, joined by lines that merge into a single arrow pointing up to "Test double": on the left, a dark gray box "Mock" with "(mock, spy)" beneath the name, and on the right, a lighter gray box "Stub" with "(stub, dummy, fake)" beneath the name.
figure-5.2: Diagram with three rounded boxes. A dark box "System under test" sits on the left. From its top, a line runs up and right, labeled "Send an email", ending in an arrow pointing at a dark box "SMTP server" on the upper right; this line is crossed by a slash marked "Mock". From a lighter box "Database" on the lower right, a line labeled "Retrieve data" runs left and up, ending in an arrow pointing into the bottom of "System under test"; this line is crossed by a slash marked "Stub". Data thus flows out of the system under test to the SMTP server and into it from the database.
figure-5.3: Hierarchy diagram. A dark rounded box "Methods" sits at the top; lines from two boxes below merge into an arrow pointing up to it. On the left is a gray box "Commands" with two white boxes stacked under it, "Incur side effects" and "No return value", and a curly brace beneath them labeled "Mocks". On the right is a lighter gray box "Queries" with two white boxes under it, "Side-effect free" and "Returns a value", and a curly brace beneath them labeled "Stubs".
figure-5.4: Two separate, non-overlapping circles. The left circle is dark gray; pointer lines from below label it both "Public API" and "Observable behavior". The right circle is lighter gray; pointer lines from above label it both "Implementation detail" and "Private API".
figure-5.5: Diagram of shapes. A dark gray circle labeled "Observable behavior" sits on the left, and a lighter gray circle labeled "Private API" on the right. A freehand outline labeled "Public API" encloses the whole dark circle and extends to the right so that it also covers part of the light circle. The part of the light circle inside the outline is labeled "Leaking implementation detail".
figure-5.6: Diagram of shapes. A freehand outline labeled "Public API" encloses two circles: a dark gray circle containing the text "Name", labeled "Observable behavior", and a lighter gray circle containing "Normalize name", labeled "Leaking implementation detail". Both circles lie fully inside the outline.
figure-5.7: Two separate, non-overlapping circles. The left circle is dark gray and contains the text "Name"; pointer lines from below label it "Public API" and "Observable behavior". The right circle is lighter gray and contains "Normalize name"; pointer lines from above label it "Implementation detail" and "Private API".
figure-5.8: A white hexagon with a dark gray circle in its center. A pointer line labels the circle "Domain (business logic)", and another pointer line labels the ring of the hexagon around the circle "Application services".
figure-5.9: Diagram of four hexagons. In the center is a white hexagon with a gray circle inside it; pointer lines label the circle "Domain (business logic)" and the surrounding hexagon area "Application services". Around it are three darker hexagons: "Message bus" at the top, "SMTP service" at the lower left, and "Third-party system" (the darkest) at the lower right. Arrows point from the central hexagon to "Message bus" and to "SMTP service", and from "Third-party system" to the central hexagon.
figure-5.10: Layered diagram. A light gray rounded box "External client" sits at the top, a dark wide rounded box "Application service" in the middle, and two dark rounded boxes "Domain class 1" and "Domain class 2" side by side at the bottom. A pair of arrows connects each neighboring level: one pointing down into the lower box and one pointing back up. The down arrow from "External client" to "Application service" is labeled "Goal (use case)", and the down arrows from "Application service" to each domain class are each labeled "Subgoal". Curly braces on the sides group the levels into tests: "Test 1" on the left spans the arrows below "External client" and the "Application service" box, "Test 2" on the left spans the arrows below "Application service" and "Domain class 1", and "Test 3" on the right spans the arrows below "Application service" and "Domain class 2".
figure-5.11: Diagram of hexagons. On the right is a white hexagon containing a large gray circle with three small dark circles inside it, connected to each other by double-headed arrows; a pointer labels these internal arrows "Intra-system". On the left are two dark hexagons: "Third-party system" at the top, with an arrow pointing from it into the white hexagon, and "SMTP service" at the bottom, with an arrow pointing from the white hexagon to it. Each of these two arrows is labeled "Inter-system".
figure-5.12: Diagram of hexagons, the same layout as figure 5.11. On the right is a white hexagon containing a large gray circle with three small dark circles connected to each other by double-headed arrows; a pointer labels these internal arrows "Implementation detail". On the left are two dark hexagons: "Third-party system" at the top, with an arrow pointing from it into the white hexagon, and "SMTP service" at the bottom, with an arrow pointing from the white hexagon to it. Each of these two arrows is labeled "Observable behavior (contract)".
figure-5.13: Diagram of hexagons. On the right is a white hexagon containing a large gray circle with two small circles inside it, labeled "Customer" and "Store" and connected by a double-headed arrow labeled "RemoveInventory()". On the upper left is a dark hexagon labeled "Third-party system" and "(external client)"; a pair of arrows connects it with the white hexagon, one pointing into the white hexagon and one pointing back to the third-party system, the latter labeled "isSuccess". On the lower left is a darker hexagon "SMTP service", with an arrow from the white hexagon to it labeled "SendReceipt()".
figure-5.14: Diagram of hexagons. In the center is a white hexagon containing a large gray circle with three small dark circles connected by double-headed arrows. On the upper left is a dark hexagon labeled "Third-party system" and "(external client)", with an arrow pointing from it into the center hexagon. On the lower left is a dark hexagon "SMTP service", with an arrow from the center hexagon to it; a pointer labels this arrow "Observable behavior (contract)". On the upper right is a dark hexagon labeled "Application database" and "(accessible only by the application)", with an arrow from the center hexagon to it. Pointer lines from both the arrow to the database and the internal arrows between the small circles lead to the label "Implementation details".
figure-6.1: Flow diagram. A wide gray arrow labeled "Input" on the left points into a rectangle labeled "Production code". On the right, a second wide gray arrow labeled "Output" leaves the rectangle; a small band around this arrow is labeled "Output verification".
